screens.title: Advanced Filtering and Pattern Matching
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how to pinpoint exactly the rows you need using advanced WHERE techniques. Pattern matching with LIKE and wildcards lets you find strings that follow a shape, such as emails from a particular domain or product names that start or end with certain letters. BETWEEN provides a concise, inclusive way to limit numeric or date ranges. IN and NOT IN let you test membership against a list of allowed or disallowed values instead of chaining many OR comparisons. NULLs behave differently from ordinary values, so you must use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL to detect missing data. Finally, logical operators — AND, OR, and NOT — let you combine these tests into powerful filters; parentheses control evaluation order and prevent subtle mistakes. Each technique matters in data preparation: selecting the right subset improves summary statistics, visualizations, and model input quality. I will walk you through syntax, concrete S Q L examples, common pitfalls such as case-sensitivity and comparing to NULL, and small design choices like when to use LOWER for case-insensitive patterns. By the end you will know how to read a requirement, choose the right operator, and write a clear, correct WHERE clause. Think about one question now: which rows would you lose if you forgot to handle NULLs explicitly?

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Advanced Filtering
Advanced Filtering and Pattern Matching
Learn how LIKE, BETWEEN, IN, NULL checks, and logical operators let you target the exact rows needed for analysis.
In this lesson
  • Pattern matching with LIKE and wildcards
  • Range filtering with BETWEEN
  • Membership and NULL handling
  • Combining conditions with AND, OR, NOT
Why this matters
Precise filters reduce noise, avoid bias from unexpected rows, and make downstream analysis reliable.
Key Takeaway

Use the right operator for the job: LIKE for patterns, BETWEEN for ranges, IN for lists, IS NULL for missing values, and logical operators to combine them safely.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you will develop specific, verifiable skills for filtering data. First, you'll learn to use the LIKE operator with its two wildcard characters, percent and underscore, so you can find strings that match a pattern rather than exact values. You'll practice writing patterns that anchor to the start, end, or internal positions of strings. Second, you'll apply BETWEEN to express inclusive ranges, which is especially useful for selecting dates or numeric bands without long comparison chains. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual to help you remember the operator's shape and use. These skills matter because they reduce query complexity and make your intent clearer to future readers of your code. As you practice, watch out for differences between databases — for example case-sensitivity — and prefer explicit normalization like LOWER when you need consistent matching. By the end of this group you will be able to explain when to use a wildcard pattern versus an equality, and you'll be ready to combine these tests into larger filters.

screens.title: LIKE and Wildcards
screens.narratorSegment: The LIKE operator lets you search for strings that follow a pattern, rather than exact equality. Two wildcards are essential: percent, which matches zero or more characters, and underscore, which matches exactly one character. For practical work, this means you can find all emails hosted at a specific domain with a single query, or find product names that fit a fixed-length pattern. For example, using WHERE email LIKE '%@example. com' returns any email that ends with @example. com regardless of the local-part. A fixed-length example uses underscore: WHERE product_name LIKE 'Jo' matches names that begin with Jo followed by exactly four characters. A common misconception is thinking LIKE always ignores case; that depends on your database. If case matters, normalize with LOWER or UPPER before matching. Another trap is forgetting to escape literal % or _ when they should be treated as characters. Practice by imagining you need every customer whose email domain is example. com — LIKE is concise and readable for that intent. Takeaway: use % when you want a flexible prefix or suffix match, and use _ when you need to control exact character positions.

keyIdea.title: Pattern matching
keyIdea.text: LIKE with % and _ offers flexible string searches; normalize case when necessary and escape wildcards when they are literal characters.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › LIKE and Wildcards
Definition
LIKE tests whether a string fits a pattern built from literals and wildcard symbols. % matches any sequence of characters; _ matches a single character.
Example
SELECT customer_id, first_name, email
FROM Customers
WHERE email LIKE '%@example.com';
% wildcard
Matches zero or more characters. Good for domain suffixes and contains checks.
_ wildcard
Matches exactly one character. Useful for fixed-length patterns.
Common mistake
Assuming LIKE is case-insensitive. Behavior varies by database; normalize with LOWER(column) if you need consistent matching.
Pattern examples and result hints
Contains 'pro'
WHERE LOWER(product_name) LIKE '%pro%'
Matches names with 'pro' anywhere; use LOWER to ignore case.
Starts with Jo and 4 more chars
WHERE product_name LIKE 'Jo____'
Matches names like 'Jordan' or 'Joseph' where underscores represent single characters.
Key takeaway
Use % for flexible spans, _ for single-character constraints, and normalize case when needed.

screens.title: Case Sensitivity and Escaping
screens.narratorSegment: Not all databases treat LIKE the same way. In some systems LIKE is case-sensitive, and in others it is not. That difference matters because a pattern that matches 'Example' in one database may miss 'example' in another. A standard approach is to normalize the column using LOWER or UPPER before applying LIKE, for example WHERE LOWER(email) LIKE '%@example. com'. This guarantees consistent behavior regardless of the database's default. Another practical issue is escaping percent or underscore characters when they are literal parts of the pattern. If a value itself contains %, you must escape it so the operator treats it as a character, not a wildcard. Many S Q L dialects offer an ESCAPE clause; the exact syntax varies between systems so check your database docs. Finally, be careful of leading or trailing spaces in your data; trimming may be necessary before matching. A concrete example: to find emails containing the literal string 100%pure@example. com you must escape the percent in your pattern. Misconception check: DON'T rely on implicit case rules for portability. Normalize text when consistent results matter. Case Sensitivity and Escaping means use lower/upper to control case-sensitivity and escape literal % or _ characters when they should not act as wildcards.. In practical terms, when like behaves differently and how to handle special characters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Case Sensitivity & Escaping
When LIKE differs across systems
Some SQL engines are case-sensitive by default; others are not. To write portable queries, normalize text with LOWER(column) or UPPER(column) before matching.
Normalized example
SELECT customer_id, email
FROM Customers
WHERE LOWER(email) LIKE '%@example.com';
Escaping example
-- Pseudocode: exact syntax depends on DB
WHERE email LIKE '%100\%pure@example.com' ESCAPE '\'
Practical tip
Normalize your data when filtering across heterogeneous systems, and document any escape strategy you use for wildcards.
Common mistake

Assuming patterns behave identically on every database. If results differ, check case rules and whether wildcards need escaping.

Key Takeaway

Normalize case for portability and escape literal % or _ characters; test patterns on sample data to confirm results.

screens.title: BETWEEN for Inclusive Ranges
screens.narratorSegment: BETWEEN is a compact, readable way to filter values inside an inclusive range. When you write WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-01-31' you select rows whose order_date is greater than or equal to January 1st and less than or equal to January 31st. That inclusivity matters with dates that include time-of-day: if your order_date includes timestamps, the final day will include all times on that date, which may or may not be what you expect. An equivalent expansion is WHERE order_date >= '2023-01-01' AND order_date = and < comparisons. A concrete example: selecting sales in January is easy with BETWEEN, but if your dataset uses timestamps you may prefer WHERE order_date >= '2023-01-01' AND order_date < '2023-02-01' to avoid missing late-night entries. Always think about inclusivity when working with dates and times. BETWEEN for Inclusive Ranges means between is inclusive at both ends; prefer explicit bounds for half-open ranges or when handling timestamps precisely.. In practical terms, select numeric or date ranges with clear, inclusive boundaries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › BETWEEN for Ranges
Concept
BETWEEN offers inclusive start and end values for numbers, dates, or strings where that semantics makes sense.
Example
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount
FROM Orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-01-31';
Equivalence
BETWEEN A AND B is the same as column >= A AND column <= B.
Timestamp caution
If values include time, the end date includes all times on that day; use half-open ranges when needed.
Alternative half-open range
To include all of January without relying on day inclusivity, write an exclusive upper bound:
WHERE order_date >= '2023-01-01' AND order_date < '2023-02-01'
Key Takeaway

BETWEEN is convenient and inclusive; choose explicit bounds if you must control endpoint semantics with timestamps.

Try this
Identify whether your date column includes time and pick BETWEEN or an explicit half-open range accordingly.

screens.title: IN and NOT IN vs OR chains
screens.narratorSegment: When you need to check whether a column equals one of several values, IN simplifies your WHERE clause and improves readability. Writing WHERE category IN ('Electronics', 'Books', 'Home Goods') is much clearer than chaining OR conditions. The NOT IN variant selects rows whose value is not any of the listed items. Use IN for membership checks and NOT IN when you want to exclude a small list of values. A concrete example from the chapter shows selecting product_name, category, price FROM Products WHERE category IN ('Electronics', 'Books', 'Home Goods'). This returns rows where category matches any of the three choices. A subtle difference to remember is that IN compares using normal equality semantics; if the column can be NULL you should be explicit with IS NULL checks, because NULL is not equal to any listed value. Misconception: NOT IN does not act as a safe null test — it simply excludes listed values. For readability and maintainability, prefer IN when checking lists, and use explicit NULL predicates when missing values must be handled. IN and NOT IN vs OR chains means in offers a compact, readable way to check membership; pair it with explicit null checks when the column may be missing values.. In practical terms, testing membership with concise syntax. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › IN and NOT IN
Concept
IN tests whether a column value appears in a supplied list. It's shorthand for multiple equality checks joined by OR.
Example
SELECT product_name, category, price
FROM Products
WHERE category IN ('Electronics', 'Books', 'Home Goods');
Readability
IN simplifies maintenance compared to long OR lists.
NOT IN
Select values not present in a list. Use with care and add explicit IS NOT NULL when necessary to handle missing values.
Equivalent OR chain
WHERE category = 'Electronics' OR category = 'Books' OR category = 'Home Goods'
Key Takeaway

Use IN for concise list checks and be explicit about NULL handling when the column may be missing values.

screens.title: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
screens.narratorSegment: NULL represents an unknown or missing value and compares differently from ordinary values. You cannot use = or!= with NULL. Any equality comparison with NULL returns UNKNOWN, which is treated as false inside WHERE. To test for missing data you must use IS NULL; to test for presence use IS NOT NULL. For example, SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name FROM Customers WHERE email IS NULL returns customers who haven't provided an email. Conversely, SELECT... WHERE email IS NOT NULL returns rows where an email exists. A common mistake is writing email = NULL or email!= NULL — these will not behave as you expect and typically return no rows. When preparing data for analysis, explicitly check for NULLs before aggregations or joins so you do not lose or miscount observations. A practical rule: whenever you see 'no value' in your data model, reach for IS NULL or IS NOT NULL instead of equality operators. This explicit check keeps filters correct and your counts reliable. IS NULL and IS NOT NULL means use is null to find absent values and is not null to find present values; equality comparisons do not work with null.. In practical terms, detecting missing values correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › IS NULL & IS NOT NULL
Concept
NULL signals missing data; comparisons using = or != don't work. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL to detect absence or presence explicitly.
Example
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name
FROM Customers
WHERE email IS NULL;
Common mistake
Writing email = NULL will not return rows with missing emails because NULL cannot be compared with =.
When to check for NULL
Check NULLs before aggregations, joins, or when a missing value changes the meaning of a filter. Explicit checks prevent silent data loss.
Key Takeaway

Treat NULL specially: use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, and never compare to NULL with = or !=.

Quick check
If a filter seems to exclude expected rows, verify whether NULL values exist and whether you used IS NULL correctly.

screens.title: Combining Conditions: AND, OR, NOT
screens.narratorSegment: Combining filters is how you build complex selection logic. AND requires all conditions to be true; OR requires at least one true; NOT negates a condition. S Q L evaluates NOT before AND, and AND before OR, so without parentheses you can get an unexpected result. For example, city = 'New York' AND is_active = TRUE AND registration_date BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND '2023-10-31' requires all three conditions to be true. Contrast that with category = 'Electronics' OR price > 1000, which selects products that meet either condition. To express exclusion use NOT combined with parentheses, e. g. WHERE NOT (category = 'Electronics' OR price > 1000). De Morgan's laws let you rewrite NOT (A OR B) as (NOT A) AND (NOT B) which can clarify logic for readers. A common error is missing parentheses in mixed AND/OR expressions. Always group related clauses so the filter reads like a sentence: test the narrow constraint first and then combine with broader ORs. A small practice: rewrite a mixed condition using parentheses and verify with sample data to confirm expected rows. Combining Conditions: AND, OR, NOT means use and, or, not with parentheses to ensure evaluation order matches your intent; apply de morgan's laws to reason about negated expressions.. In practical terms, constructing precise logical filters with correct precedence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › AND / OR / NOT
Rules and precedence
NOT has highest precedence, then AND, then OR. Parentheses override this order and make intent explicit.
Examples
-- All must be true
WHERE city = 'New York' AND is_active = TRUE
  AND registration_date BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND '2023-10-31';

WHERE category = 'Electronics' OR price > 1000;

-- Using NOT with parentheses

NOT (A OR B) is equivalent to (NOT A) AND (NOT B). Rewriting expressions can make intent clearer when negating complex logic.
Misconception

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging Filters
screens.narratorSegment: When a filter returns unexpected results, the cause is usually one of a few classic mistakes. First, check for NULLs: equality comparisons with NULL always fail, so rows with missing values may disappear silently. Second, operator precedence can change meaning — without parentheses, AND may bind more tightly than OR, producing broader or narrower result sets than intended. Third, case-sensitivity on LIKE can hide matches in some databases; normalize text to avoid surprises. Fourth, BETWEEN includes endpoints; if timestamps exist you might be excluding late-day events unless you use a half-open interval. Another debugging technique is stepwise filtering: apply one predicate at a time and inspect intermediate counts or sample rows. If a combined filter returns zero rows, remove the last predicate and re-run to identify which condition filtered everything out. Use small result sets or LIMIT to test quickly. A practical habit: include comments in your S Q L that state your intention so reviewers can see why a constraint was included. These practices make your filters robust and maintainable. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to pinpoint exactly the rows you need using advanced WHERE techniques. Pattern matching with LIKE and wildcards lets you find strings that follow a shape, such as emails from a particular domain or product names that start or end with certain letters. BETWEEN provides a concise, inclusive way to limit numeric or date ranges. IN and NOT IN let you test membership against a list of allowed or disallowed values instead of chaining many OR comparisons. NULLs behave differently from ordinary values, so you must use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL to detect missing data. Finally, logical operators — AND, OR, and NOT — let you combine these tests into powerful filters; parentheses control evaluation order and prevent subtle mistakes. Each technique matters in data preparation: selecting the right subset improves summary statistics, visualizations, and model input quality. I will walk you through syntax, concrete S Q L examples, common pitfalls such as case-sensitivity and comparing to NULL, and small design choices like when to use LOWER for case-insensitive patterns. By the end you will know how to read a requirement, choose the right operator, and write a clear, correct WHERE clause. Think about one question now: which rows would you lose if you forgot to handle NULLs explicitly?

Over the next screens you will develop specific, verifiable skills for filtering data. First, you'll learn to use the LIKE operator with its two wildcard characters, percent and underscore, so you can find strings that match a pattern rather than exact values. You'll practice writing patterns that anchor to the start, end, or internal positions of strings. Second, you'll apply BETWEEN to express inclusive ranges, which is especially useful for selecting dates or numeric bands without long comparison chains. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual to help you remember the operator's shape and use. These skills matter because they reduce query complexity and make your intent clearer to future readers of your code. As you practice, watch out for differences between databases — for example case-sensitivity — and prefer explicit normalization like LOWER when you need consistent matching. By the end of this group you will be able to explain when to use a wildcard pattern versus an equality, and you'll be ready to combine these tests into larger filters.

These next objectives guide how to combine filters and avoid common errors. You will practice combining conditions using AND, OR, and NOT, and you will learn how parentheses change evaluation order. Operator precedence means NOT typically applies first, then AND, then OR, which can lead to unintended rows when conditions are chained without grouping. You will also explore small but important practical details: how case-sensitivity affects LIKE patterns across database systems and when to use LOWER or UPPER to normalize text for matching. Finally, you will complete hands-on tasks that require composing multiple operators with parentheses to mirror precise selection criteria. Each objective includes a short why-this-matters note and a compact mnemonic so you can apply the concept immediately when preparing datasets for analysis. By practicing these skills you will avoid logical mistakes that silently include or exclude rows and you'll write WHERE clauses that are both correct and easy to read.

The LIKE operator lets you search for strings that follow a pattern, rather than exact equality. Two wildcards are essential: percent, which matches zero or more characters, and underscore, which matches exactly one character. For practical work, this means you can find all emails hosted at a specific domain with a single query, or find product names that fit a fixed-length pattern. For example, using WHERE email LIKE '%@example. com' returns any email that ends with @example. com regardless of the local-part. A fixed-length example uses underscore: WHERE product_name LIKE 'Jo' matches names that begin with Jo followed by exactly four characters. A common misconception is thinking LIKE always ignores case; that depends on your database. If case matters, normalize with LOWER or UPPER before matching. Another trap is forgetting to escape literal % or _ when they should be treated as characters. Practice by imagining you need every customer whose email domain is example. com — LIKE is concise and readable for that intent. Takeaway: use % when you want a flexible prefix or suffix match, and use _ when you need to control exact character positions.

Not all databases treat LIKE the same way. In some systems LIKE is case-sensitive, and in others it is not. That difference matters because a pattern that matches 'Example' in one database may miss 'example' in another. A standard approach is to normalize the column using LOWER or UPPER before applying LIKE, for example WHERE LOWER(email) LIKE '%@example. com'. This guarantees consistent behavior regardless of the database's default. Another practical issue is escaping percent or underscore characters when they are literal parts of the pattern. If a value itself contains %, you must escape it so the operator treats it as a character, not a wildcard. Many S Q L dialects offer an ESCAPE clause; the exact syntax varies between systems so check your database docs. Finally, be careful of leading or trailing spaces in your data; trimming may be necessary before matching. A concrete example: to find emails containing the literal string 100%pure@example. com you must escape the percent in your pattern. Misconception check: DON'T rely on implicit case rules for portability. Normalize text when consistent results matter. Case Sensitivity and Escaping means use lower/upper to control case-sensitivity and escape literal % or _ characters when they should not act as wildcards.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

BETWEEN is a compact, readable way to filter values inside an inclusive range. When you write WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-01-31' you select rows whose order_date is greater than or equal to January 1st and less than or equal to January 31st. That inclusivity matters with dates that include time-of-day: if your order_date includes timestamps, the final day will include all times on that date, which may or may not be what you expect. An equivalent expansion is WHERE order_date >= '2023-01-01' AND order_date = and < comparisons. A concrete example: selecting sales in January is easy with BETWEEN, but if your dataset uses timestamps you may prefer WHERE order_date >= '2023-01-01' AND order_date < '2023-02-01' to avoid missing late-night entries. When you need to check whether a column equals one of several values, IN simplifies your WHERE clause and improves readability. Writing WHERE category IN ('Electronics', 'Books', 'Home Goods') is much clearer than chaining OR conditions. The NOT IN variant selects rows whose value is not any of the listed items.
